name: Circle Packing

lumenary.blurb: Circles that never overlap, each as large as the room allows. The picture decides how big they may grow and what colour they take.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with a clear contrast between dark and light

why: Packing circles into a space is the problem of fitting round things as tightly as they will go. By letting the picture set how large each circle may grow, the same process draws a portrait out of bubbles, where large circles gather in the chosen tones and small ones fill the gaps.
how: Try random points and ask how big a circle could be centred there.
Take the smallest of four limits: the radius the picture asks for, the distance to the four walls, and the distance to every neighbour minus its radius and the gap.
If the answer is at least the smallest allowed radius, place the circle.
Use a grid of cells as wide as the largest circle so only the nine nearest cells are searched.
The wanted radius is r_min × 1.6 + (r_max − 1.6 r_min) f^0.9, where f is the tone, so large circles gather where the picture asks.
history: Apollonius of Perga described circles tangent to three others in the third century BC. René Descartes wrote a relation among four touching circles in 1643, rediscovered by Frederick Soddy in 1936 as a poem. The circle packing theorem, proved by Koebe in 1936 and later developed by Thurston in the 1980s, links packings to networks of points.
uses: Bubble charts and hierarchical data views
terms: Placing shapes in a space without overlap.
A fractal made by filling gaps between circles with more circles.
paragraphs: The program fills the picture with circles that never overlap, each as large as the room allows. It tries random points, and at each one asks how big a circle could be. The answer is the smallest of four things: the radius the picture asks for, the distances to the four walls, and the distance to every neighbouring circle minus its radius and the gap. If the answer is at least the smallest allowed radius, the circle is placed. A grid with cells the size of the largest circle means only the nine nearest cells need to be searched, and the number of attempts grows with the area divided by the smallest circle’s area.

The picture decides the radius it asks for. With size following the light or the dark, the wanted radius is r_min × 1.6 + (r_max − 1.6 r_min) f^0.9, where f is the tone (or one minus it), so large circles gather in the chosen tones and small ones fill everything else. Each circle takes the picture’s colour at its centre. Circles can be drawn as flat discs, as rings whose stroke is 0.28 of the radius, or as glossy beads with a radial gradient lit from the upper left, brightened ×1.4 + 50 at the highlight and darkened to 0.62 at the rim.

equations.tex: r=\min\Big(r_{\text{want}},\ x,\ W-x,\ y,\ H-y,\ \min_k\big[\lVert\mathbf p-\mathbf p_k\rVert-r_k-g\big]\Big),\qquad \text{accept if } r\ge r_{\min}
equations.note: The largest circle that fits at point p, given the other circles (centres p_k, radii r_k) and the gap g.
The radius the picture asks for; f is the tone, or 1 − tone when the dark parts should be large.

presets.text: Large circles gathering in the light parts invert the look.
Ring mode makes bubbles with open centres.
Tiny minimum circles fill almost every gap.
